reading.rtitle: The Tense That Says the Work Is Still Running
paras: Every senior leader is asked the same question in interviews and in reviews: what are you working on? The weak answer gives a list. The strong answer gives a list plus a clock. 'We have been piloting the new review process since March' tells your listener three things at once: the work started, it is still going, and you know exactly how long it has been going. That is the present perfect continuous, and in a status conversation it does more work than any other tense in English.

The form is simple: have or has, then been, then the -ing verb. 'The team has been ramping up capacity for two quarters.' 'I have been keeping up with the safety literature since I moved into the role.' Two small words carry the duration: for plus a length of time, and since plus a starting point. For six months, for two quarters, for a year. Since March, since 2019, since I took the role. Brazilians almost always reach for the present continuous here and say 'I am working here for six years', which sounds to an American ear like a plan for next week. The fix is one word: have been.

There is a second form, and the difference is not decoration. The present perfect simple points at the result, usually a number: 'We have piloted four teams.' The continuous points at the activity and its duration: 'We have been piloting since March.' Use the simple form when you want the score, and the continuous when you want the effort. Two verbs refuse the continuous completely, because they describe a state and not an activity: know and understand. 'I have known him for twenty years' is correct. 'I have been knowing him' is not English at all, and it is one of the fastest ways to sound like a beginner in a room where everything else you say is senior.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The present perfect continuous shows that work started, is still going, and has lasted a measurable time -- while the simple form points at the result.
The present continuous is the correct tense for saying how long you have worked somewhere.
The continuous form can be used with every English verb, including know and understand.

gapfill.text: have / has + been + verb-ing. Use for with a length of time (for two quarters) and since with a starting point (since March). Use the simple form -- have piloted, have delivered -- when you want the number. Never use the continuous with know or understand.

bank.label: Useful sentences for a status update
items: We have been piloting the new review process since March.
The team has been ramping up capacity for two quarters.
Adoption has been climbing every week since the launch.
I have been keeping up with the safety literature since I moved into this role.
The workload has been growing faster than headcount.
We have been iterating on the same design for three months.
We have piloted four teams so far, and two are already live.
I have known the platform team for twenty years.

forms.title: Five moves with have been + -ing
cards: 'The team has been ramping up capacity.' Three parts, always in that order, and the -ing verb never changes.
'We have been iterating on the same design for three months.' For answers 'how long?' -- never 'when?'.
'We have been piloting the process since March.' Since answers 'starting when?' -- a date, a year, or a whole clause: since I took the role.
'We have piloted four teams so far.' The result and the score take the simple form; the effort and the duration take the continuous.
'I have known the platform team for twenty years.' Never 'I have been knowing'. The same applies to understand, believe and own.

items.situation: An interviewer asks how long you have been in your current role. Answer in one sentence with a duration.
tips: I have been leading the platform group for two years.
I have been running this program since 2023.

items.situation: A board member asks what your team is working on right now. Give the activity and how long it has been running.
tips: We have been piloting a new review process since March.
We have been iterating on the same design for three months.

items.situation: Someone asks for the number, not the story. Give the score.
tips: We have piloted four teams so far, and two are already live.
We have delivered three of the five milestones.

items.situation: Explain why you need more people, using a trend that is still happening.
tips: The workload has been growing faster than headcount.
Adoption has been climbing every week, and the team has not been growing with it.

items.situation: An interviewer asks how you stay current in AI safety. Answer with a duration, and avoid the continuous where it does not belong.
tips: I have been keeping up with the safety literature since I moved into this role.
I have known most of that research community for years, and I have been reading their papers every week.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
In three sentences, give a status update on one real program: one sentence with for, one with since, and one with the simple form for a number.
Round 2 -- The one-minute update
Give a one-minute status update on a real program: what has been running, how long, what has already been delivered, and what is still in progress.
Round 3 -- Under pressure
Deliver the same update in thirty seconds, and add one sentence about a trend that is still moving -- workload, adoption or headcount.
Curveball
The interviewer asks 'And how long have you known that team?' Answer with the simple form, then switch back to the continuous for what you have been doing with them.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model status update
list: Model: 'We have been piloting the new review process since March, and adoption has been climbing every week since the launch. The platform team has been ramping up capacity for two quarters, because the workload has been growing faster than headcount. We have piloted four teams so far, and two of them are already live. We have been iterating on the same design for three months, and I have been keeping up with the safety literature since I moved into this role. I have known most of that group for twenty years, so the conversations move quickly.'
With since: We have been piloting the new review process since March... / ...since I moved into this role.
With for: The platform team has been ramping up capacity for two quarters. / We have been iterating on the same design for three months.
A trend still moving: Adoption has been climbing every week. / The workload has been growing faster than headcount.
Simple form for the number: We have piloted four teams so far, and two of them are already live.
State verb, simple only: I have known most of that group for twenty years.
answerkey.note: Continuous = the activity and how long it has lasted. Simple = the result and the number. For + length of time, since + starting point. Know and understand never take the continuous.

listenings.text: Thanks for making time. Here is where the program actually stands, and I will keep it to two minutes. We have been piloting the new review process since March, so we are now in month five, and adoption has been climbing every week since the launch. We have piloted four teams so far, and two of them are already live in production. The platform group has been ramping up capacity for two quarters, and they need to, because the workload has been growing faster than headcount for most of this year. We have been iterating on the same intake design for three months, and honestly, that is the part I am least happy about. What I can tell you is that nothing has stalled. Everything on this list is still moving. I have known this engineering group for twenty years, and I have not seen them work at this pace before.

Let me give you the one correction I make most often with senior candidates from Brazil. Someone asks how long you have been in the role, and the answer comes back as I am working here for six years. Every word in that sentence is a real English word, and the sentence still lands wrong, because to an American ear the present continuous points at right now or at next week, never at six years of history. Say I have been working here for six years and the whole answer changes shape. Now the second half of the correction, and this one is subtler. Use for with a length of time and since with a starting point. For six years, since 2019. And when the interviewer wants a number rather than a story, drop the continuous completely. We have delivered three of the five milestones. That is a score, so it takes the simple form. Finally, two verbs will never take the continuous, no matter how long the situation has lasted. I have known this team for twenty years. Never I have been knowing.
